why.correct: Gases cross between air and blood only in the respiratory zone: the alveoli and the tiny airways whose walls carry alveoli. Everything above is conducting zone.
options: The nasal cavity and its conchae are conducting zone. Their thick, glandular, ciliated lining warms, moistens and filters air but does not exchange gases with blood.
The larynx is conducting zone. It guards the airway and makes sound; its walls are far too thick for gases to cross.
Correct. Only the respiratory zone, where alveolar walls are a single thin layer of cells, exchanges gases with the blood.
The trachea and the larger air tubes are conducting zone. They deliver air to the lungs; their walls of mucosa and cartilage are too thick for gas exchange.

why.correct: The conducting zone runs from the nose through the pharynx, larynx and trachea to the smallest air tubes without alveoli. Alveoli are the respiratory zone.
options: Correct. The nasal cavity filters, warms and humidifies air but exchanges no gas with blood.
Correct. The pharynx carries air (and in its lower two parts, food) but exchanges no gas with blood.
Alveoli are where gas exchange happens, so they are the respiratory zone.
Correct. The larynx conducts air into the trachea and makes sound.
Correct. The trachea conducts air down to the lungs.

why.correct: The part of the pharynx behind the nasal cavity and above the mouth is the nasopharynx. Only air passes through it.
options: Correct. The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity, above the level of the mouth.
The oropharynx lies lower, behind the mouth.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest part, behind the larynx.
The nasal vestibule is the entrance just inside each naris, at the front of the nose, not behind it.

why.correct: The leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage standing up behind the base of the tongue is the epiglottis. It tips back over the opening of the larynx when you swallow.
options: The thyroid cartilage is the large shield in the front wall of the larynx, lower down.
Correct. This flap at the top of the larynx is the epiglottis.
The vestibular folds are folds of mucous membrane inside the larynx, just above the vocal folds.
The hyoid bone is the U-shaped bone in front, below the jaw; the larynx hangs from it.

why.correct: The midline ridge where the two plates of the thyroid cartilage meet is the laryngeal prominence, the Adam's apple.
options: The cricoid cartilage is the ring below the thyroid cartilage, not the ridge on its front.
The epiglottis is the flap rising above and behind the hyoid bone.
Correct. This is the laryngeal prominence of the thyroid cartilage.
The body of the hyoid bone is the bar of bone at the top of the larynx.

why.correct: The glottis is the pair of vocal folds together with the gap between them. It is the narrowest part of the adult airway.
options: Correct. The V-shaped opening between the vocal folds, with the folds themselves, is the glottis.
The epiglottis is the flap at the front of the larynx, seen here near the base of the tongue.
The laryngopharynx is the part of the throat around and behind the larynx, not the opening inside it.
The nasopharynx is far higher, behind the nasal cavity.

why.correct: Mouth breathing bypasses the nasal cavity, where the conchae make air swirl against warm, blood-rich, mucus-covered surfaces. Air therefore arrives colder, drier and carrying more particles.
options: Faster air has less contact time with warm surfaces, so it is less warmed, not more.
Correct. Skipping the nasal cavity skips most of the warming, humidifying and filtering.
The pharynx adds some warmth and moisture, but the nasal cavity, with its conchae and dense blood supply, does most of the work, so skipping it changes the air.
The trachea is conducting zone. No oxygen crosses into the blood there, however the air arrives.

why.correct: Air enters the nares, passes through the nasal cavity, then down the three parts of the pharynx from top to bottom, and forward into the larynx, which opens into the trachea.
options: The nares are the two openings of the nose.
The nasal cavity lies behind the nares and opens back into the pharynx.
The nasopharynx is the top part of the pharynx, behind the nasal cavity.
The oropharynx lies behind the mouth, below the nasopharynx.
The laryngopharynx is the lowest part, behind the larynx.
The larynx opens off the front of the laryngopharynx and leads down into the trachea.

why.correct: The nasopharynx lies above the mouth. When you swallow, the muscular back part of the roof of your mouth lifts and seals it, so food does not enter it.
options: The oropharynx lies behind the mouth, so swallowed food passes through it.
The laryngopharynx carries food down to the esophagus as well as air to the larynx.
Correct. The nasopharynx is sealed off during swallowing and carries only air.
The nasopharynx is sealed off during swallowing, so only the lower two parts carry food.

why.correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerves, branches of the vagus nerve, supply most of the small muscles that move the arytenoid cartilages and vocal folds. They run up beside the thyroid gland, so thyroid surgery can injure one and leave that vocal fold unable to close.
options: Correct. Without its nerve supply, the fold cannot be brought to the midline, so air leaks past and the voice is breathy.
The muscles that lift the hyoid bone raise the larynx during swallowing; they do not open or close the vocal folds.
The vestibular folds do not make sound, so damage to one would not stop a vocal fold moving.
A cricoid injury is unlikely in thyroid surgery and would not explain a single paralyzed fold.

why.correct: Food passes through the oropharynx and laryngopharynx but not the nasopharynx. Stratified squamous epithelium has many layers, so cells lost to abrasion are replaced from below.
options: The pharynx is not an absorbing surface; a thick stratified lining would absorb poorly anyway.
No part of the pharynx exchanges gases with blood; it is all conducting zone.
Stratified squamous epithelium in the pharynx has no cilia. Food is moved by the skeletal muscle of the pharyngeal wall.
Correct. The lining matches the job: abrasion-resistant where food passes, ciliated where only air passes.

why.correct: The vocal folds must first close, so that the contracting abdominal wall muscles build up pressure against a sealed airway. Only then do the folds open suddenly and release the blast.
options: Correct step. Sensory receptors in the lining of the larynx, trachea and large air tubes detect the irritant.
Correct step. The vagus nerve carries the sensory signal to the brainstem.
Correct step. A deep breath in loads the lungs with air for the blast.
This is the wrong step. The folds close while the muscles contract, so pressure can build; with open folds the air would leak out gently.
Correct step. The sudden opening releases a high-speed blast.

why.correct: As the larynx rises, with its folds already closed, the epiglottis tips down and back over its opening, a second cover.
options: Correct. The epiglottis covering the laryngeal opening is the outer seal, added after the folds inside have closed.
The cricoid cartilage is a rigid ring of the larynx, in front of the start of the esophagus; it does not open for food.
The conchae are fixed shelves of bone in the nasal cavity; they do not move or close anything.
The vocal folds close during swallowing; they vibrate only when air is pushed through them to make sound.

why.correct: Smoke slows the cilia and, over years, destroys ciliated cells while goblet cells multiply. More mucus is made and little is carried up, so it pools until coughing clears it.
options: The mucus still traps particles; the problem is that it is not being carried away.
Smoking makes goblet cells multiply, so he makes more mucus, not less.
Correct. With the mucociliary escalator failing, coughing becomes the main way out.
A cough can be triggered more easily in a smoker, but that would not explain why mucus builds up in the first place.

why.correct: The conchae break the airstream into narrow, turbulent channels. Heavier particles cannot follow the air around the bends and land on the sticky mucus that covers the conchae.
options: The mucosa's mucus does contain antibodies, but they act on particles trapped in the mucus, not in the air.
Correct. Turbulence throws particles against the mucus-covered surfaces.
The conchae increase surface area and turbulence; their benefit is contact with the lining, not speed.
Cilia in the nasal cavity sweep mucus backward toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed, not forward out of the nose.

why.correct: The vocal folds, or true vocal cords, contain elastic vocal ligaments. Air pushed between them sets them vibrating, which makes sound.
options: The vestibular folds, the false vocal cords, lie above the vocal folds. They help close the larynx but do not make sound.
The epiglottis is a single flap of elastic cartilage; it covers the laryngeal opening but does not vibrate to make voice.
Correct. The lower pair, the true vocal cords, make sound.
The nasal septum is a partition in the nose, not a structure of the larynx.

why.correct: Pitch depends on how fast the folds vibrate. Muscles that stretch the folds tighter and thinner make them vibrate faster, raising the pitch, as with a tightened guitar string.
options: A wider swing of the folds makes the sound louder, not higher.
Open vocal folds do not vibrate at all, so no voice is produced.
More pressure beneath the folds makes the sound louder; the question holds loudness constant.
Correct. Tighter, thinner folds vibrate faster, producing a higher pitch.

why.correct: The cricoid cartilage is a complete ring, narrow in front and tall behind like a signet ring. It sits on top of the trachea.
options: The thyroid cartilage is two plates joined in front; it is open at the back.
Correct. The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring.
The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap, not a ring.
The arytenoid cartilages are small paired pieces at the back of the larynx.

why.correct: Each auditory tube runs from the nasopharynx to the middle ear. Microorganisms from an infected nose and throat can travel up it, especially in young children, whose tubes are short and nearly horizontal.
options: Correct. The auditory tube links the nasopharynx to the middle ear.
The paranasal sinuses drain into the nasal cavity, not into the ear.
The nasal vestibule is the skin-lined entrance to the nose; it has no connection to the ear.
The laryngopharynx leads to the larynx and esophagus; it has no opening to the ear.

why.correct: Irritation of the nasal mucosa is carried to the brainstem by the trigeminal nerve, which carries touch and pain from the face and nasal cavity.
options: The vagus nerve carries the sensory signal for a cough, from the larynx, trachea and large air tubes, not from the nose.
The phrenic nerve is a motor nerve to the diaphragm. It does not carry sensation from the nose.
The glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensation from the back of the tongue and the oropharynx, not from the nasal cavity.
Correct. The trigeminal nerve carries the irritation signal from the nasal mucosa.

why.correct: Of the two folds inside the larynx, the upper one is the vestibular fold, the false vocal cord.
options: The vocal fold is the lower of the two folds.
Correct. The upper fold is the vestibular fold.
The epiglottis is the flap at the top of the larynx, well above these folds.
The pharyngeal tonsil lies in the back wall of the nasopharynx, far above the larynx.

why.correct: The hollow in the front edge of the left lung, where the heart lies, is the cardiac notch.
options: Correct. Only the left lung has a cardiac notch, because the heart lies mostly left of the midline.
The hilum is on the mediastinal (inner) surface, where the bronchus and vessels enter, not a notch in the front edge.
The oblique fissure is a deep groove that separates the lobes; it runs diagonally across the lung.
The apex is the narrow top of the lung, which rises above the clavicle.

why.correct: The right lung has three lobes. The one between the horizontal and oblique fissures is the middle lobe.
options: The right superior lobe lies above the horizontal fissure.
Correct. The middle lobe lies between the two fissures of the right lung.
The left lung is on the other side of the figure, and it has no middle lobe.
The left superior lobe is on the other side of the figure, above the left oblique fissure.

why.correct: A respiratory bronchiole is a small airway with a few alveoli budding from its wall. It is the first airway of the respiratory zone.
options: The terminal bronchiole is the airway just before it, higher up, wrapped in smooth muscle and without alveoli.
An alveolar duct comes after it; its walls are almost entirely alveolar openings.
Correct. This branch carries scattered alveoli, so it is a respiratory bronchiole.
A tertiary bronchus is a much larger airway with cartilage plates, many branchings earlier.

why.correct: The alveolar duct is the short passage at the end of a respiratory bronchiole whose walls are made of alveolar openings. It leads into the alveolar sacs.
options: Alveolar pores are small holes in the walls between neighboring alveoli, not passages leading to them.
An alveolar sac is the grape-like cluster of alveoli at the end of the duct.
The terminal bronchiole is higher up, before any alveoli appear.
Correct. This passage between the respiratory bronchiole and the alveolar sacs is an alveolar duct.

why.correct: The narrow gap between the visceral pleura on the lung and the parietal pleura on the chest wall is the pleural cavity. It holds only a thin film of pleural fluid.
options: The mediastinum is the central compartment between the two lungs, holding the heart and great vessels.
Correct. This thin space between the two pleural layers is the pleural cavity.
The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart, not the lung.
A bronchus is an airway inside the lung; this space lies outside the lung, next to the chest wall.

why.correct: The trachea divides into primary bronchi, then secondary bronchi (one per lobe), tertiary bronchi (one per segment), smaller bronchi and bronchioles, terminal bronchioles (the last conducting airways), respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli.
options: The primary bronchi are the first branches, one to each lung.
Each lobe has its own secondary bronchus.
Each bronchopulmonary segment has its own tertiary bronchus.
The terminal bronchiole is the last airway of the conducting zone.
The respiratory bronchiole is the first airway with alveoli in its wall.
The alveolar duct leads into the alveolar sacs.

why.correct: The right primary bronchus is wider, shorter and more nearly vertical than the left, so an object falling down the trachea tends to continue straight into it.
options: The left primary bronchus leaves the trachea at a sharper angle to pass under the aortic arch, so objects enter it less often.
Correct. The straighter, wider right primary bronchus is the usual site.
The nasopharynx lies above the larynx; an object that has been breathed in has already passed below it.
The carina is the ridge between the two primary bronchi. An object touching it triggers a cough but does not usually stay there.

why.correct: The carina is a keel-shaped ridge formed by the last tracheal cartilage, pointing up between the openings of the two primary bronchi. Its lining is very sensitive and triggers a strong cough.
options: Correct. The carina sits at the split of the trachea.
The trachea begins just below the cricoid cartilage of the larynx; the carina is at the other end.
The smooth muscle at the back of the trachea is the trachealis muscle.
The notch in the left lung is the cardiac notch.

why.correct: The open back of each ring is closed only by the trachealis muscle and connective tissue, a soft wall that gives way when the esophagus behind it swells with food. The rigid front and sides still keep the airway open.
options: The C shape concerns the back wall, not the length. Elastic tissue between the rings lets the trachea lengthen as you move your neck.
The trachea and esophagus are separate tubes; air does not pass between them through the back wall.
Correct. The soft back wall lets the esophagus expand into it.
The bronchi form where the trachea divides at the carina; the C shape of the rings has nothing to do with branching.

why.correct: Type II alveolar cells are cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant, the film that lowers surface tension, and act as the repair cells of the alveolar wall, turning into new type I cells.
options: Type I cells form the thin gas-crossing wall. They rarely, if ever, divide and do not secrete surfactant.
Alveolar macrophages engulf particles and microorganisms; they do not build the wall.
Capillary endothelial cells line the blood side of the respiratory membrane, not the air side.
Correct. Type II cells secrete surfactant and replace lost type I cells.

why.correct: The respiratory membrane is a type I alveolar cell, the fused basement membranes of that cell and the capillary, and a capillary endothelial cell: about 0.5 µm in total.
options: Correct. The flattened type I cell is the air side of the barrier.
Correct. The two basement membranes are fused into one layer.
Correct. The endothelial cell of a continuous capillary is the blood side.
Type II cells are scattered and cover only about 5% of the surface; the barrier where gases cross is formed by type I cells.
The visceral pleura covers the outside of the lung. Oxygen in the alveoli never crosses it.

why.correct: Diffusion rate falls as diffusion distance rises. A thicker respiratory membrane makes oxygen take longer to cross, so less crosses during the brief time each red blood cell spends in an alveolar capillary.
options: Correct. A longer diffusion distance slows diffusion.
Oxygen still has to cross the whole thickened barrier; extra fluid lengthens the path rather than helping.
Nothing here changes the gradient or the area, but distance also sets diffusion rate, and it has increased.
Oxygen still moves from alveolar air, where there is more of it, into the blood; only its rate changes.

why.correct: Terminal bronchioles are the last purely conducting airways. The respiratory bronchioles beyond them carry the first alveoli.
options: Tertiary bronchi are conducting airways, but many branchings come after them.
Respiratory bronchioles have alveoli in their walls, so they begin the respiratory zone.
Correct. The terminal bronchiole ends the conducting zone.
Alveolar ducts are lined with alveolar openings, so they are respiratory zone.

why.correct: The left lung has two lobes, superior and inferior, so the left primary bronchus gives off two secondary bronchi. Three is the right lung's number.
options: Correct step. The carina marks the division of the trachea.
Correct step. Each primary bronchus enters its lung at the hilum.
This is the wrong step. The left lung has two lobes and so two secondary bronchi.
Correct step. Tertiary (segmental) bronchi each supply one bronchopulmonary segment.
Correct step. Branching continues down to the terminal bronchioles, the end of the conducting zone.

why.correct: After the terminal bronchiole comes the respiratory bronchiole, the first airway with alveoli in its wall, which leads into alveolar ducts.
options: Tertiary bronchi come well before the terminal bronchioles.
Alveolar pores are holes between neighboring alveoli, not a step along the airway.
The primary bronchus is near the start of the tree, just below the trachea.
Correct. The respiratory bronchiole links the terminal bronchiole to the alveolar ducts.

why.correct: This is pleurisy: the pleural layers are inflamed and rub together. The parietal pleura, supplied by the intercostal and phrenic nerves, is very sensitive to pain; the lung and visceral pleura are not.
options: The visceral pleura is inflamed too, but it has no pain fibers of that kind, so it does not produce sharp pain.
Lung tissue, including the alveolar walls, is not sensitive to sharp pain.
Correct. The parietal pleura's pain fibers fire as the inflamed layers rub with each breath.
The bronchial arteries supply the airway walls; they are not the source of pleuritic pain.

why.correct: The bronchial arteries are small systemic branches, mostly from the thoracic aorta, that supply the airway walls, connective tissue and visceral pleura.
options: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the alveolar capillaries for gas exchange.
Correct. The bronchial arteries feed the lung's own tissue.
Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood away from the lungs to the left atrium; they do not feed the airway walls.
Bronchial veins drain blood away from the larger airways.

why.correct: The lungs have a second, systemic blood supply. The bronchial arteries, branches of the aorta, keep feeding the airway walls and connective tissue even when a pulmonary artery branch is blocked.
options: Veins do not reverse to supply tissue; pulmonary veins carry blood toward the left atrium.
Alveolar pores pass air between alveoli, not blood.
Lung tissue is living tissue and needs oxygen like any other.
Correct. The double blood supply is what protects the tissue.

why.correct: Alveolar macrophages move over the alveolar surface and through its walls, engulfing particles and microorganisms beyond the reach of cilia and mucus.
options: Correct. They are the alveoli's cleaners, sometimes called dust cells.
Alveoli have no goblet cells or mucus; mucus stops higher up the tree.
Type I alveolar cells form the gas-crossing wall.
There are no cilia in the alveoli.

why.correct: Bronchioles have no cartilage and a thick layer of smooth muscle for their size, so nothing holds them open when that muscle contracts.
options: The trachea is held open by its cartilage rings; only its back wall has smooth muscle.
Primary bronchi are held open by cartilage, which resists narrowing.
Correct. Without cartilage, bronchiole diameter is set by smooth muscle alone.
Alveolar sacs have only scattered strands of smooth muscle near their entrances.

why.correct: Alveolar pores are small openings in the walls between neighboring alveoli. Air can pass sideways through them from alveoli whose own airways are open.
options: Correct. Alveolar pores let air move sideways between neighbors.
The pleural cavities lie outside the lungs and hold only a film of fluid, no air.
Bronchial veins carry blood, not air.
Tracheal cartilages hold the trachea open; they are nowhere near the alveoli.

why.correct: The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) and two fissures. The left lung has two lobes, one fissure and a cardiac notch for the heart.
options: This reverses the lobe counts: the right lung has three lobes, the left two.
Correct. Three lobes on the right; two lobes and a cardiac notch on the left.
Both lungs have a hilum, where the bronchus, vessels and nerves enter.
Visceral pleura covers both lungs.

why.correct: Boyle's law: P₂ = P₁ × V₁ ÷ V₂ = 760 × 500 ÷ 400 = 950 mm Hg. A smaller volume gives a higher pressure.
options: 608 comes from 760 × 400 ÷ 500, the ratio upside down. That would be the answer for an expansion, not a squeeze.
860 comes from adding the 100 mL change to 760. Pressure and volume are related by a ratio, not by adding the difference.
660 comes from subtracting the 100 mL change from 760. Pressure changes by a ratio, and a squeeze raises it.

why.correct: P₂ = 760 × 2.500 ÷ 2.505 = 758.5 mm Hg, which is about 1.5 mm Hg below the 760 mm Hg outside. Air will flow in down that gradient.
options: Correct. 760 × 2.500 ÷ 2.505 ≈ 758.5 mm Hg, about −1.5 relative to atmospheric.
A larger volume lowers the pressure, so the sign must be negative.
−5 treats the 5 mL volume change as if it were a pressure change in mm Hg. Use Boyle's law to find the pressure.
Alveolar pressure equals atmospheric pressure only when no air is flowing and volume is steady. Here the volume has just risen.

why.correct: Intrapleural pressure falls during inspiration, from about −4 to about −6 mm Hg by 2 seconds, the end of breathing in.
options: 0 is where alveolar pressure sits at the end of breathing in, not intrapleural pressure.
−1 is the lowest alveolar pressure, reached at mid-inspiration.
Correct. At the end of inspiration intrapleural pressure is about −6 mm Hg.
−4 is the intrapleural pressure at rest, at the start of breathing in and the end of breathing out.

why.correct: Airflow is driven by the gradient between atmospheric and alveolar pressure. At about 1 second, alveolar pressure is about −1 mm Hg, the steepest inward gradient, and the volume curve is rising most steeply.
options: At 0 seconds alveolar pressure is still 0, so there is no gradient and no flow yet.
Correct. The largest pressure difference gives the fastest inflow.
At 2 seconds alveolar pressure is back to 0: the gradient, and so the flow, has stopped. Volume is largest because flow has just ended.
At 3 seconds alveolar pressure is above atmospheric, so air is flowing out, not in.

why.correct: Air flows only down a pressure gradient. At 2 seconds, alveolar pressure is back to 0, equal to atmospheric pressure, so there is no gradient and flow stops.
options: Transpulmonary pressure is at its largest at 2 seconds, about 6 mm Hg, holding the lungs at their larger size.
At 2 seconds intrapleural pressure is still about −6; it climbs back toward −4 only during breathing out.
Correct. With alveolar and atmospheric pressures equal, nothing drives airflow.
A quiet breath uses only a small part of the lungs' stretch; a deep breath can add liters more. Flow stops because the gradient is gone.

why.correct: Transpulmonary pressure = alveolar pressure − intrapleural pressure = 0 − (−4) = 4 mm Hg.
options: −4 is the intrapleural pressure itself. Transpulmonary pressure is the difference between alveolar and intrapleural pressure.
0 is the alveolar pressure at rest. Subtract the intrapleural pressure from it.
6 mm Hg is the transpulmonary pressure at the end of breathing in, at 2 seconds.
Correct. 0 − (−4) = 4 mm Hg.

why.correct: Nerve signal, muscle contraction, larger thorax, lower intrapleural pressure, lung expansion, lower alveolar pressure by Boyle's law, and finally airflow down the gradient.
options: Neurons in the brainstem send the signal down the phrenic nerves (C3 to C5).
The diaphragm contracts, flattening and moving down.
The thorax gets longer, and the external intercostals also widen it.
The chest wall moves out, and the pleural film holding the lung to it is pulled harder, so intrapleural pressure falls.
Transpulmonary pressure rises, and the lungs stretch.
The larger alveolar volume lowers alveolar pressure, and air flows in down the gradient.

why.correct: Quiet expiration is passive. No muscle contracts to push air out; the lungs and chest wall recoil on their own. The internal intercostals join in only during forced expiration.
options: Correct step. Expiration begins when the inspiratory muscles relax.
This is the wrong step. The internal intercostals contract only in forced expiration, not in a quiet breath.
Correct step. Elastic recoil shrinks the lungs and the thorax.
Correct step. By Boyle's law, the smaller alveolar volume raises alveolar pressure.
Correct step. Air flows out down the gradient until the pressures are equal.

why.correct: By Boyle's law, the enlarged alveoli hold the same air in more space, so alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows in down the gradient.
options: Intrapleural pressure falls during inspiration, and stays below atmospheric in quiet breathing.
Airways do not pump air. Contraction of airway smooth muscle would narrow them and hinder flow.
Surfactant lowers surface tension; it does not move air.
Correct. The drop in alveolar pressure creates the gradient that drives inflow.

why.correct: Air in the pleural cavity raises intrapleural pressure toward atmospheric. Transpulmonary pressure disappears, the lung's own recoil collapses it, and the chest wall's movements no longer expand it.

variables.name: Intrapleural pressure
variables.why: Air enters until the pressure in the cavity approaches atmospheric pressure, so it rises from about −4 toward 0.

variables.name: Transpulmonary pressure
variables.why: Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus intrapleural pressure; with intrapleural pressure near 0, it falls toward 0.

variables.name: Volume of the left lung
variables.why: Without transpulmonary pressure to hold it open, the lung recoils toward its hilum and collapses.

variables.name: Airflow into the left lung with each breath
variables.why: The collapsed lung is no longer held to the chest wall, so it barely expands when the chest does, and little air flows into it.

why.correct: Narrowed bronchioles raise resistance by the fourth-power rule, so each breath moves less air unless the muscles generate a larger pressure difference. Breathing out is hit hardest, because the airways narrow further as the lungs shrink.

variables.name: Bronchiole radius
variables.why: Smooth muscle contraction, a swollen wall and mucus in the lumen all shrink the radius.

variables.name: Airway resistance
variables.why: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ r⁴, so a smaller radius raises it steeply.

variables.name: Airflow for the same pressure difference
variables.why: Flow = ΔP ÷ R. With R higher and ΔP unchanged, flow falls.

variables.name: Pressure difference the breathing muscles must create
variables.why: To move enough air through higher resistance, the muscles must contract harder and create a larger gradient, recruiting accessory muscles.

variables.name: Time needed to breathe out fully
variables.why: Airways narrow further as the lungs shrink during expiration, so air leaves slowly and some is trapped.

why.correct: A tension pneumothorax collapses one lung and keeps building pressure in the chest. That squeezes the great veins and heart, so venous return, cardiac output and blood pressure fall, and the baroreceptor reflex speeds the heart. Removing the air with a needle and a chest tube reverses it.

variables.name: Pressure in the right pleural cavity
variables.why: Air is added with every breath and none leaves, so the pressure climbs above atmospheric.

variables.name: Venous return to the heart
variables.why: The rising pressure pushes the mediastinum aside and compresses the great veins and the heart, so less blood returns to the right atrium.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Less venous return means less filling (lower preload), so stroke volume and cardiac output fall.

variables.name: Arterial blood pressure
variables.why: Blood pressure depends on cardiac output; with output falling, pressure falls. This is obstructive shock.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Falling arterial pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, and the cardiovascular center raises sympathetic drive to the heart.

why.correct: Air entering through the wound raises intrapleural pressure to atmospheric. Transpulmonary pressure falls to zero, and the lung's own elastic recoil collapses it, even though its airways are open.
options: Correct. With intrapleural pressure at atmospheric, there is no pressure difference across the lung wall to hold the lung open against its recoil.
With the lung collapsed and its airways open, alveolar pressure stays near atmospheric. The problem is the pressure outside the lung, not inside it.
The question says the diaphragm contracts normally, so the phrenic nerve is working.
Surfactant lines the inside of the alveoli; a wound in the chest wall does not reach it, and losing it would stiffen the lung, not collapse it all at once.

why.correct: Type II alveolar cells usually make enough surfactant only by about 34 to 36 weeks. Without it, the water lining her alveoli has high surface tension, compliance is low, and many alveoli collapse at the end of each breath and must be reopened with great effort.
options: Air in a pleural cavity would collapse a lung, but nothing here suggests a pneumothorax; her whole lungs are stiff.
Narrow bronchioles raise resistance, which slows airflow; they would not make the lung tissue itself stiff.
Fewer elastic fibers would make the lungs easier to inflate, not stiffer: compliance would rise, not fall.
Correct. Surfactant deficiency means high surface tension and low compliance.

why.correct: Compliance = ΔV ÷ ΔP = 0.6 L ÷ (7 − 4) mm Hg = 0.6 ÷ 3 = 0.2 L per mm Hg.
options: 1.8 comes from multiplying 0.6 by 3. Compliance is volume divided by pressure change.
Correct. 0.6 L ÷ 3 mm Hg = 0.2 L/mm Hg.
5 comes from 3 ÷ 0.6, the division upside down.
0.086 comes from dividing by the final pressure, 7, instead of by the change in pressure, 3.

why.correct: Resistance is proportional to 1 ÷ r⁴. If r falls to one third, r⁴ falls to (1/3)⁴ = 1/81, so resistance rises 81-fold.
options: 3 would apply if resistance depended on radius alone. It depends on the fourth power of the radius.
9 uses the square of the radius change. Resistance depends on the fourth power.
27 uses the cube of the radius change. Resistance depends on the fourth power.
Correct. 3⁴ = 81.

why.correct: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist. It binds beta-2 receptor proteins on airway smooth muscle, the muscle relaxes, the bronchioles widen, and resistance falls steeply because of the fourth-power rule.

Carbon monoxide holds hemoglobin in its high-affinity shape, shifting the curve left.
