why.correct: Working muscle raises carbon dioxide, H+ and temperature. Through the Bohr effect and heat, hemoglobin's affinity falls and the curve shifts right, so hemoglobin gives up more oxygen exactly where it is being used.

variables.name: PCO2 of the blood in the muscle capillaries
variables.why: Faster aerobic respiration makes more carbon dioxide, which diffuses into the blood.

variables.name: Blood pH in the muscle capillaries
variables.why: Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which releases H+, and working muscle adds acid of its own, so H+ rises and pH falls.

variables.name: Hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
variables.why: More carbon dioxide, more H+ and higher temperature all stabilize hemoglobin's tense shape: the curve shifts right.

variables.name: P50
variables.why: A lower affinity means a higher PO2 is needed to half-saturate hemoglobin.

variables.name: Oxygen released per 100 mL of blood
variables.why: A lower tissue PO2 on the steep part of the curve, plus a right shift, lowers the saturation of blood leaving the muscle.

why.correct: Red blood cells lose 2,3-BPG during storage. Without it, hemoglobin stays in its high-affinity shape, so the curve shifts left: the cells load fully in the lungs but release less at tissue PO2 until they rebuild their 2,3-BPG over about a day.
options: Stored cells keep their hemoglobin; his 99% saturation shows it is carrying oxygen.
Correct. Low 2,3-BPG raises affinity and impairs unloading.
Stored blood is refrigerated, and a right shift would increase unloading, not reduce it.
Once in his circulation, the transfused blood equilibrates with his alveolar air like the rest of his blood.

why.correct: A standard two-light oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so it reads near normal. PO2 measures only dissolved oxygen, which carbon monoxide does not change. Meanwhile, much of the hemoglobin is carrying carbon monoxide. A CO-oximeter measures carboxyhemoglobin directly.
options: Carbon monoxide does not raise PO2; it leaves it normal while cutting the oxygen carried on hemoglobin. The oximeter reads high because it mistakes carboxyhemoglobin for oxyhemoglobin.
Cold fingers give weak or failed readings, but they do not explain a normal PO2 as well.
Faulty burning makes carbon monoxide because there is too little oxygen, not extra oxygen.
Correct. Neither measurement sees the hemoglobin occupied by carbon monoxide.

why.correct: Carbon monoxide leaves the lungs and dissolved oxygen alone, so PO2 and the pulse oximeter look normal. It cuts oxygen content, shifts the curve left and blocks mitochondria, so tissues go short of oxygen. The cardiovascular system responds with a faster heart rate, and the cells produce more lactate.

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: Her lungs and breathing are normal, so the oxygen dissolved in her plasma is unchanged; carbon monoxide acts on hemoglobin.

variables.name: SpO2 on a standard pulse oximeter
variables.why: The device reads carboxyhemoglobin as if it were oxyhemoglobin, so the display stays near normal.

variables.name: Arterial oxygen content
variables.why: Carbon monoxide occupies 30% of the heme sites, which then cannot carry oxygen.

variables.name: Oxygen released to the tissues at a given tissue PO2
variables.why: Carbon monoxide shifts the curve left, so the remaining oxygen is held more tightly.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Tissues short of oxygen, and the sympathetic response to her symptoms, drive the heart faster, raising cardiac output.

variables.name: Blood lactate
variables.why: Cells short of oxygen, and cells whose mitochondria are directly blocked by carbon monoxide, turn to anaerobic metabolism.

why.correct: Equal content does not mean equal delivery. Carbon monoxide on some heme sites holds the rest of each hemoglobin in its high-affinity shape, so patient A releases less of the oxygen she carries. Patient B's curve is normal, or shifted right by extra 2,3-BPG.
options: Anemia lowers oxygen content, not arterial PO2, which depends on the lungs.
Content is equal, but unloading is not; the shape of the curve decides how much is released.
Delivery depends on the oxygen content and how readily hemoglobin releases it; patient B's hemoglobin releases normally.
Correct. The left shift impairs unloading in patient A.

why.correct: Carbon monoxide and oxygen compete for the same iron in heme. Raising PO2 about fivefold drives more oxygen onto the sites as carbon monoxide comes off, so carboxyhemoglobin falls by half in about 1 to 1.5 hours instead of 4 to 6 hours on room air.
options: Carbon monoxide leaves the body unchanged through the lungs; the blood does not convert it.
Correct. Competition at the heme sites speeds its removal.
Oxygen does not shift the curve right; the treatment works by competition for binding sites.
Nothing in the heart filters gases; carbon monoxide leaves by diffusing out in the lungs.

why.correct: Cyanide blocks the electron transport chain, so cells cannot use the oxygen delivered to them. Oxygen stays in the blood, and venous PO2 stays high. That is histotoxic hypoxia.
options: Hypoxemic hypoxia means a low arterial PO2, and his is normal.
Anemic hypoxia means low oxygen content, and his is normal.
Stagnant hypoxia comes from slow flow, which lets tissues take more oxygen and lowers venous PO2; his venous PO2 is high.
Correct. Cells that cannot use oxygen leave it in the venous blood.

why.correct: Her arterial blood carries a normal amount of oxygen, but too little of it flows to her feet each minute. That is stagnant, or circulatory, hypoxia. The slow-moving blood gives up more of its oxygen, so her venous PO2 is low.
options: Correct. Low flow delivers too little oxygen.
Her arterial PO2 is normal, so too little oxygen is not getting into her blood.
Nothing is stopping her cells from using oxygen; they are not receiving enough.
Her hemoglobin is normal, so her blood's oxygen content is normal.

why.correct: The low total pressure lowers the PO2 of the air he breathes, so too little oxygen gets into his blood: a low arterial PO2 is hypoxemia, and the resulting tissue hypoxia is hypoxemic (hypoxic) hypoxia.
options: His hemoglobin is normal; the problem is too little oxygen for it to pick up.
His cells can use oxygen normally; they are not receiving enough.
Correct. The low arterial PO2 marks hypoxemic hypoxia.
His circulation is normal, so slow flow is not the problem.

why.correct: Ventilation brings oxygen to the alveoli; it diffuses into plasma and then onto hemoglobin; the circulation carries it to the tissue; conditions there shift and lower saturation so hemoglobin releases it; and it diffuses down its gradient into the cell, where the electron transport chain uses it.

Carbon dioxide and H+ stabilize hemoglobin's tense, low-affinity shape. That is what shifts the curve right and makes hemoglobin release more oxygen. A shift toward the relaxed, high-affinity shape would do the opposite.
options: This step is right. Aerobic respiration makes carbon dioxide, and working muscle makes acid.
This step is right. This is the basis of the Bohr effect.
This is the error. The shift is toward the tense, low-affinity shape.
This step is right. Lower affinity is a right shift.
This step is right. A right-shifted curve gives a lower saturation at any PO2.

why.correct: P50 is the PO2 at 50% saturation, normally about 27 mm Hg. If more PO2 is needed to half-fill hemoglobin, its affinity is lower: a right shift.
options: Correct. A higher P50 is a right shift.
A left shift means higher affinity, so hemoglobin is half full at a lower PO2: the P50 falls.
P50 refers to half saturation, not full saturation.
27 mm Hg is the normal P50 value itself, not the saturation level that defines it.

why.correct: Saturation is a percentage of the hemoglobin present. Her 7 g is 99% loaded, but her oxygen content is only about 7 × 1.34 × 0.99 + 0.3 ≈ 9.6 mL per 100 mL, half of normal. That is anemic hypoxia.
options: A full load on half the normal hemoglobin carries about half the normal oxygen.
A 99% reading is accurate here: nearly every hemoglobin molecule she has is loaded.
Her lungs load her hemoglobin almost completely, as the 99% shows. The problem is the amount of hemoglobin.
Correct. Saturation is not content.

why.correct: Fetal hemoglobin has two alpha and two gamma chains. The gamma chains bind 2,3-BPG weakly, so its affinity for oxygen is higher and its curve lies to the left, with a P50 of about 19 mm Hg.
options: Correct. Gamma chains and weak 2,3-BPG binding give it a higher affinity.
Fetal hemoglobin has four heme groups, just like adult hemoglobin.
Both kinds keep the alpha chains; fetal hemoglobin swaps beta for gamma, and binding more 2,3-BPG would lower its affinity.
Fetal hemoglobin carries oxygen normally; carbon monoxide binds both kinds.

why.correct: About 70% of the carbon dioxide in blood travels as bicarbonate. It is made inside red blood cells by carbonic anhydrase and carried mostly in the plasma after the chloride shift.
options: Carbaminohemoglobin carries about 20–23%, a real but smaller share.
Correct. Bicarbonate carries about 70%.
Dissolved carbon dioxide is only about 7–10%, even though carbon dioxide is far more soluble than oxygen.
Carbonic acid exists only for an instant before it splits into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, so almost none is present at any moment.

why.correct: Without an enzyme, carbon dioxide reacts with water too slowly to reach equilibrium in the second or so blood spends in a capillary. Carbonic anhydrase sits inside red blood cells, so that is where almost all the bicarbonate is made.
options: Correct. The uncatalyzed reaction is slow, and the enzyme that speeds it is inside red blood cells.
Carbon dioxide dissolves in plasma well; about 7–10% of it travels that way.
Plasma pH is about 7.4, close to neutral, and carbonic acid can form at that pH. The limit is speed, not pH.
Chloride does not block the reaction. It takes part only in the exchange for bicarbonate across the red blood cell membrane.

why.correct: Inside the red blood cell, carbonic anhydrase converts carbon dioxide to carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate. The bicarbonate then moves into the plasma. This route carries about 70% of the carbon dioxide.
options: Dissolved carbon dioxide is the smallest share, about 7–10%.
Carbon dioxide cannot stay in the tissue cell: it diffuses out down its partial pressure gradient and must reach the lungs in the blood.
Correct. Conversion to bicarbonate carries about 70%.
Binding to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin carries about 20–23%, the middle share.

why.correct: Carbonic anhydrase is the enzyme in red blood cells that speeds the reaction of carbon dioxide with water by thousands of times.
options: Band 3 is the membrane carrier protein that swaps bicarbonate for chloride. It moves the product; it does not make it.
Hemoglobin binds the hydrogen ions and some carbon dioxide, but it is not the enzyme that forms carbonic acid.
Correct. Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3.
Chloride ions enter in exchange for bicarbonate. They do not catalyze anything.

why.correct: Carbonic anhydrase is what lets red blood cells turn carbon dioxide into bicarbonate quickly. Blocking it leaves more carbon dioxide dissolved, which raises PCO2 in the blood and tissues, and it slows the chloride shift because there is less bicarbonate to exchange.

variables.name: Bicarbonate made inside red blood cells
variables.why: Without the enzyme, carbon dioxide reacts with water too slowly to reach equilibrium while the blood is in the capillary, so less bicarbonate forms.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide carried as dissolved gas
variables.why: Carbon dioxide that is not converted to bicarbonate stays dissolved, so the dissolved share rises.

variables.name: PCO2 of the blood leaving the tissue
variables.why: Dissolved carbon dioxide is the form that sets PCO2. With more of it left unconverted, PCO2 rises.

variables.name: Chloride moving into red blood cells
variables.why: The chloride shift swaps chloride in for bicarbonate out. With less bicarbonate made, less chloride moves in.

why.correct: In the tissues, carbon dioxide enters the blood, is converted to bicarbonate in red blood cells, and the bicarbonate moves into the plasma by the chloride shift. In the lungs every step reverses: bicarbonate re-enters the red blood cell, is converted back to carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide diffuses into the alveoli.
Band 3 swaps one bicarbonate ion for one chloride ion. Both are negative ions, so the exchange keeps the charge across the membrane unchanged. This is the chloride shift.
options: Correct. Chloride enters as bicarbonate leaves.
Sodium is a positive ion. Swapping it for bicarbonate, a negative ion, would change the charge across the membrane; band 3 exchanges negative ions only.
Potassium is also a positive ion and is kept inside cells by the sodium–potassium pump, not exchanged for bicarbonate.
Oxygen is leaving the red blood cell in a systemic capillary, and it crosses by simple diffusion, not through band 3.

why.correct: Band 3 is a passive exchanger. Bicarbonate and chloride each move down their own concentration gradients, which is facilitated diffusion, and no ATP is used.
options: This step is right. The PCO2 in the plasma is higher than inside the red blood cell, so carbon dioxide diffuses in.
This step is right. Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3.
This step is right. Carbonic acid splits almost at once.
This is the error. The chloride shift is facilitated diffusion through band 3, not an ATP-driven pump.
This step is right. Chloride moves in as bicarbonate moves out, one for one.

why.correct: Her cells keep making carbon dioxide, but none is breathed out, so PCO2 rises. More carbon dioxide drives CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− to the right, more hydrogen ions are freed, and pH falls.
options: PCO2 does rise, but more carbon dioxide makes more hydrogen ions, which lowers pH rather than raising it.
Without breathing, carbon dioxide cannot leave, so PCO2 cannot fall.
This is what happens when someone breathes fast and deep: carbon dioxide is blown off, and pH rises. A breath-hold does the opposite.
Correct. Carbon dioxide builds up, and the extra carbonic acid lowers pH.

why.correct: This is the Haldane effect in the lungs. Oxyhemoglobin holds hydrogen ions less well than deoxyhemoglobin, so it releases them. They combine with bicarbonate to form carbonic acid, which carbonic anhydrase converts to carbon dioxide and water. Oxyhemoglobin also releases the carbon dioxide it held as carbaminohemoglobin.
options: Oxygen does not react with bicarbonate. The link runs through hemoglobin and the hydrogen ions it releases.
Correct. Released hydrogen ions drive the reaction back toward carbon dioxide.
Carbonic anhydrase is always active. It speeds the reaction in whichever direction the concentrations push it; oxygen does not switch it on.
Chloride does leave the red blood cell in the lungs, but only in exchange for bicarbonate coming in. It does not carry carbon dioxide.

why.correct: In the tissues, carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate inside the red blood cell and the chloride shift brings chloride in. The hydrogen ions made at the same time are bound to hemoglobin, so they do not count as free particles. The cell ends up with more dissolved particles, water moves in by osmosis, and the cell swells slightly. Venous hematocrit is a few percent higher for this reason.
options: Losing oxygen changes hemoglobin's shape slightly, but not its volume enough to swell the cell. The swelling comes from water entering.
Venous pressure is lower than arterial pressure, not higher.
Carbon dioxide stays dissolved or chemically bound in blood; it does not form bubbles.
Correct. More osmotically active particles inside the cell draw in water.

why.correct: Carbon dioxide binds the free amino groups at the ends of the globin chains, not the heme iron, so it does not take oxygen's place. Deoxyhemoglobin forms carbaminohemoglobin more readily, which is part of the Haldane effect. It carries about 20–23% of the carbon dioxide, and it forms directly, without an enzyme.
options: Correct. The binding site is the amino groups of globin.
Correct. Deoxyhemoglobin binds carbon dioxide more readily, one cause of the Haldane effect.
About 70% is the share carried as bicarbonate. Carbaminohemoglobin carries about 20–23%.
The heme iron is where oxygen (and carbon monoxide) binds. Carbon dioxide binds the protein chains instead.
Carbamino binding happens directly between carbon dioxide and the amino groups. Carbonic anhydrase speeds the bicarbonate reaction, not this one.
Correct. Because it binds a different site, it does not compete with oxygen for the iron, although it lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen slightly.

why.correct: This is the Haldane effect. At the same PCO2, deoxygenated blood carries more carbon dioxide, because deoxyhemoglobin binds hydrogen ions more readily (pulling more carbon dioxide into bicarbonate) and forms carbaminohemoglobin more readily.
options: PCO2 sets only the dissolved carbon dioxide. The total the blood holds also depends on how much is converted to bicarbonate and bound to hemoglobin, which depends on oxygenation.
This reverses the Haldane effect: oxyhemoglobin binds less carbon dioxide and fewer hydrogen ions.
Correct. Less oxygen on hemoglobin means more carbon dioxide carried at the same PCO2.
Red blood cells already contain carbonic anhydrase, and dissolved carbon dioxide needs no enzyme at all.

why.correct: Breathing more than the body's carbon dioxide production requires lowers PCO2. The carbonic acid reaction runs to the left, hydrogen ions are consumed, and pH rises.

variables.name: PCO2
variables.why: He is breathing out carbon dioxide faster than his cells make it, so the carbon dioxide in his alveoli and arterial blood falls.

variables.name: Hydrogen ion concentration
variables.why: Less carbon dioxide pulls CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− to the left, which uses up hydrogen ions.

variables.name: pH
variables.why: pH rises when free hydrogen ions fall.

why.correct: In the lungs, bicarbonate is being converted back to carbon dioxide inside red blood cells, so bicarbonate inside falls. Bicarbonate from the plasma moves in through band 3, and chloride moves out: the chloride shift in reverse.
options: This is the direction in the systemic capillaries, where bicarbonate is being made inside the red blood cell.
Correct. The exchange reverses in the lungs.
Chloride is an ion dissolved in body fluids; it cannot be exhaled as a gas.
Band 3 works in both directions, driven by the gradients. In the lungs, the gradients are reversed, so the shift reverses.

why.correct: Hemoglobin is unloading oxygen in the same capillary where hydrogen ions are being made, and deoxyhemoglobin binds hydrogen ions more readily than oxyhemoglobin. It buffers most of them, so the free hydrogen ion concentration rises only a little.
options: Correct. Buffering by deoxyhemoglobin keeps venous pH close to arterial pH.
The chloride shift moves bicarbonate out, not hydrogen ions. Chloride enters in exchange for bicarbonate.
Carbonic anhydrase speeds the reaction that makes hydrogen ions; it does not remove them.
Hydrogen ions are not a gas and cannot be exhaled. Only carbon dioxide leaves through the lungs.

why.correct: Difference = 53 − 48 = 5 mL per 100 mL. Cardiac output 8,000 mL/min is 80 lots of 100 mL. 80 × 5 = 400 mL/min.
options: 40 comes from using 8 lots of 100 mL instead of 80: 8 L is 8,000 mL, which is 80 lots of 100 mL.
Correct. 80 × 5 mL = 400 mL of carbon dioxide per minute.
4,000 comes from multiplying 8,000 by 5 without dividing by 100: the 5 mL is per 100 mL of blood, not per mL.
4.2 L/min is about the total carbon dioxide in 8 L of venous blood (53 mL per 100 mL × 80), not the amount unloaded. Only the difference between venous and arterial blood is unloaded.

why.correct: This is the Haldane effect. Deoxyhemoglobin buffers hydrogen ions better, which pulls more carbon dioxide into bicarbonate, and it forms carbaminohemoglobin more readily. The more oxygen the muscle takes, the more carbon dioxide the blood can take away.
options: Carbonic anhydrase is not switched on by low oxygen. It is always active and speeds the reaction in the direction the concentrations push it.
Correct. Unloading oxygen raises the blood's capacity for carbon dioxide.
Muscle cells release carbon dioxide, which becomes bicarbonate inside red blood cells. They do not secrete bicarbonate into the blood.
A warmer liquid does dissolve gases less well, but that would lower carbon dioxide loading, not raise it.

why.correct: Neurons of the pre-Bötzinger complex, near the top of the ventral respiratory group in the medulla oblongata, fire in rhythmic bursts on their own, even when isolated from the rest of the brain. Many textbooks give the dorsal respiratory group this role; current evidence points to the pre-Bötzinger complex.
options: Correct. This cluster in the medulla generates the rhythm.
The pneumotaxic center fine-tunes the rhythm by switching off inspiration earlier. Breathing continues when the pons is cut away.
The carotid bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors. They change breathing but do not generate its rhythm.
The motor cortex can override breathing voluntarily, but you keep breathing in your sleep and in coma, when it is not driving the muscles.

why.correct: The pneumotaxic center, the pontine respiratory group, is the upper of the two areas in the pons. It sends inhibiting signals that switch off inspiration.
options: Correct. This is the pneumotaxic center in the upper pons.
The apneustic center lies below the pneumotaxic center, lower in the pons.
The dorsal respiratory group is in the medulla oblongata, not the pons.
The ventral respiratory group is in the medulla oblongata, not the pons.

why.correct: The dorsal respiratory group lies toward the back of the medulla oblongata. It receives sensory input through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves and drives inspiration.
options: The apneustic center is in the pons, above the medulla.
The ventral respiratory group lies toward the front of the medulla, in front of the dorsal group.
Correct. This is the dorsal respiratory group.
The pneumotaxic center is in the upper pons.

why.correct: The ventral respiratory group lies toward the front of the medulla oblongata. It contains the pre-Bötzinger complex and the neurons that drive forced expiration and the accessory muscles.
options: The dorsal respiratory group sits behind the ventral group, toward the back of the medulla.
Correct. This is the ventral respiratory group.
The pneumotaxic center is in the upper pons.
The apneustic center is in the lower pons, above the medulla.

why.correct: The carotid bodies sample arterial blood directly and respond within seconds to a fall in pH from any cause. Hydrogen ions cross the blood–brain barrier poorly, so the central chemoreceptors are slow to sense acid that is not carried in as carbon dioxide.
options: Lung stretch receptors respond to inflation of the lungs, not to blood chemistry.
Central chemoreceptors respond to hydrogen ions in the brain's fluid, which come mainly from carbon dioxide crossing the barrier. Hydrogen ions from the blood cross only slowly.
Irritant receptors respond to dust, smoke and fumes in the airways, not to blood pH.
Correct. The peripheral chemoreceptors sense the low arterial pH first.

why.correct: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to the partial pressure of oxygen, which depends on the oxygen dissolved in plasma, not on how much hemoglobin carries. In anemia, arterial PO2 is normal, so the carotid bodies are not strongly stimulated.
options: Anemia does not damage the carotid bodies. They are working normally; they simply sense PO2, which is normal.
Correct. The sensors read PO2, not oxygen content.
Central chemoreceptors do not sense oxygen at all, and they do not block signals from the carotid bodies.
Low oxygen content does not act on the respiratory centers directly at this level; there is no signal telling them oxygen content is low.

why.correct: Hyperventilation lowers arterial PCO2, which raises pH. Low PCO2 constricts brain arterioles, the alkalosis lowers free calcium, and the central chemoreceptors reduce their drive, which pushes breathing back toward normal once the emotional drive fades.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: She is breathing out carbon dioxide faster than her cells make it.

variables.name: Arterial pH
variables.why: Less carbon dioxide means less carbonic acid and fewer hydrogen ions.

variables.name: Blood flow to the brain
variables.why: Low carbon dioxide constricts the arterioles in the brain, which is why she feels lightheaded.

variables.name: Free calcium in the plasma
variables.why: In alkalosis, more calcium binds to albumin and other plasma proteins, leaving less free, which causes tingling and hand spasms.

variables.name: Drive from her central chemoreceptors
variables.why: With less carbon dioxide crossing into the brain's fluid, its hydrogen ions fall and the central chemoreceptors fire less.

why.correct: In the first hours, low oxygen raises ventilation through the carotid bodies, and the fall in PCO2 raises pH, which restrains breathing. Over days, the kidneys correct the pH, the brake comes off and ventilation rises further. Over weeks, more red blood cells raise the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

variables.name: Ventilation in the first hours
variables.why: Low arterial PO2 stimulates the carotid bodies, which drive the respiratory centers.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2 in the first hours
variables.why: The extra ventilation blows off carbon dioxide faster than it is made.

variables.name: Blood pH in the first hours
variables.why: Less carbon dioxide means fewer hydrogen ions, and the central chemoreceptors act as a brake on further breathing.

variables.name: Ventilation after one week, compared with the first hours
variables.why: The kidneys excrete bicarbonate and the cerebrospinal fluid's bicarbonate falls, so pH returns toward normal, the central brake is released, and the carotid bodies become more sensitive.

variables.name: Blood pH after one week, compared with the first hours
variables.why: Losing bicarbonate in the urine brings the raised pH back toward normal.

variables.name: Hematocrit after three weeks, compared with the first hours
variables.why: Low oxygen makes the kidneys release more erythropoietin, which speeds erythropoiesis.

why.correct: Exercise raises carbon dioxide production, and the nervous system raises ventilation and cardiac output to match. Because ventilation keeps pace, arterial PCO2 stays about normal even though venous blood from the muscles carries more carbon dioxide. The drive comes largely from the motor cortex and proprioceptors, not from a change in arterial PCO2 or PO2.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide production by muscle
variables.why: Working muscle runs more cellular respiration, which makes more carbon dioxide.

variables.name: Ventilation
variables.why: Signals from the motor cortex and proprioceptors, fine-tuned by the chemoreceptors, raise ventilation to match carbon dioxide production (hyperpnea).

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Ventilation rises in step with carbon dioxide production, so arterial PCO2 stays near 40 mm Hg in moderate exercise.

variables.name: PCO2 of venous blood leaving the working muscles
variables.why: The muscles add more carbon dioxide to each liter of blood passing through them.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Sympathetic drive raises heart rate and contractility, and the muscle pump raises venous return.

why.correct: The carotid bodies respond to low arterial PO2, high arterial PCO2 and low arterial pH. They sense PO2, not oxygen content, so anemia with a normal PO2 does little. Cerebrospinal fluid is sensed by the central chemoreceptors, and lung inflation by lung stretch receptors.
options: Correct. A PO2 below about 60 mm Hg stimulates them strongly.
Correct. They respond quickly to a rise in PCO2.
Correct. They respond to acid in arterial blood from any cause.
In anemia, arterial PO2 is normal, so the carotid bodies are not strongly stimulated.
Cerebrospinal fluid bathes the central chemoreceptors, not the carotid bodies, which sit in the neck.
Lung inflation is sensed by lung stretch receptors, which inhibit inspiration through the vagus nerves.

why.correct: At constant carbon dioxide production, arterial PCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation. Half the ventilation doubles the PCO2: 40 × 2 = 80 mm Hg.
options: 20 mm Hg is what happens if alveolar ventilation doubles. Less ventilation raises PCO2.
PCO2 cannot stay the same: the same carbon dioxide production is being cleared by half as much air.
60 mm Hg adds half of 40 instead of doubling it. The relationship is inverse proportion, not a 50% rise.
Correct. Halving alveolar ventilation doubles arterial PCO2.

why.correct: Hypoventilation and hyperventilation are defined by arterial PCO2, not by rate. Her PCO2 is above 45 mm Hg, so she is hypoventilating. With very shallow breaths, much of each breath only fills the dead space and never reaches the alveoli, so alveolar ventilation is low despite the fast rate.
options: A fast rate is not the same as hyperventilation. Hyperventilation lowers PCO2 below 35 mm Hg; hers is high.
If the fast rate made up for the small breaths, her PCO2 would be normal. At 58 mm Hg it is not.
Correct. A high PCO2 defines hypoventilation.
In hyperpnea, ventilation matches carbon dioxide production and PCO2 stays normal. Hers is high.

why.correct: Hyperventilation lowers PCO2 a lot but barely raises blood oxygen, because hemoglobin is already nearly saturated. Underwater, PCO2 climbs from a lower starting point and takes longer to reach the level that forces a breath. Meanwhile oxygen keeps falling, and he loses consciousness from low oxygen first.
options: Hemoglobin is already about 97% saturated at rest, so hyperventilating adds very little oxygen. Oxygen does not suppress breathing in a healthy person.
Correct. The carbon dioxide alarm was delayed while oxygen ran out.
Cold water stimulates breathing, often causing a gasp; it does not switch off the carotid bodies. His problem began before the dive.
A breath-hold of this length does not damage the brainstem. The blackout comes from low oxygen, not from injury to the centers.

why.correct: With the respiratory centers depressed, alveolar ventilation falls well below what his carbon dioxide production requires. PCO2 rises (hypercapnia), more carbonic acid forms, and pH falls. His arterial PO2 also falls.
options: Low PCO2 and high pH are the pattern of hyperventilation, the opposite of what slow breathing causes.
Correct. Hypoventilation causes hypercapnia and a fall in pH.
Breathing 5 times a minute cannot clear his carbon dioxide production, so the gases cannot stay normal.
A high PCO2 forms more carbonic acid, which lowers pH rather than raising it.

why.correct: Studies show ventilation falls only a little when such patients receive oxygen. Most of the rise in PCO2 comes from worsening ventilation–perfusion mismatch, as oxygen reopens constricted arterioles in poorly ventilated lung, and from the Haldane effect, as oxygenated hemoglobin holds less carbon dioxide. The response is to aim for a target saturation, often 88–92%, never to withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient.
options: This is the older hypoxic-drive explanation that many exams still expect. The evidence shows her ventilation would fall only slightly; it is not the main cause.
Oxygen does not damage the central chemoreceptors. They are less responsive because they have adapted to her long-term high PCO2.
Correct. V/Q worsening and the Haldane effect explain most of the rise.
Oxygen does not block carbonic anhydrase. The enzyme works regardless of oxygen level.

why.correct: This is the Hering–Breuer (inflation) reflex. Stretch receptors in the airway smooth muscle send signals through the vagus nerves that inhibit inspiration, limiting tidal volume. In adults it acts mainly when tidal volume is large, as here.
options: Correct. The reflex cuts inspiration short when the lungs are well inflated.
Contraction of airway smooth muscle is a response to irritant receptors, triggered by dust, smoke or fumes, not by stretch.
Signals from the lung stretch receptors inhibit inspiration; they do not drive the diaphragm harder.
The stretch reflex acts on the respiratory centers, not on the carotid bodies.

why.correct: Carbon dioxide crosses into the brain's fluid and forms hydrogen ions, which the central chemoreceptors sense. They drive the respiratory centers, which send more signals down the phrenic nerves. Deeper, faster breathing raises alveolar ventilation, and PCO2 falls: negative feedback.
The central chemoreceptors do not sense oxygen. They respond to hydrogen ions in the brain's fluid. Low oxygen is sensed only by the peripheral chemoreceptors, mainly the carotid bodies.
options: This step is right. A PO2 below about 60 mm Hg is a strong stimulus.
This step is right. The carotid bodies are the main oxygen sensors.
This step is right. The carotid bodies signal through the glossopharyngeal nerves.
This is the error. Central chemoreceptors do not respond to low oxygen.
This step is right. The respiratory centers increase their output.
This step is right. More ventilation raises alveolar and arterial PO2, reducing the stimulus.

why.correct: Motor neurons from spinal segments C3–C5 leave through the phrenic nerves to the diaphragm.
options: Correct. The phrenic nerves supply the diaphragm.
The vagus nerves carry sensory signals from the lungs and aortic bodies to the brainstem; they do not drive the diaphragm.
The glossopharyngeal nerves carry sensory signals from the carotid bodies to the medulla.
The intercostal nerves drive the intercostal muscles, not the diaphragm.

why.correct: In the first hours, low PCO2 raises the pH of the blood and brain fluid, and the central chemoreceptors restrain breathing. Over days, the kidneys excrete bicarbonate and the cerebrospinal fluid's bicarbonate falls, so pH moves back toward normal and the brake comes off. The carotid bodies also become more sensitive to low oxygen.
options: Hematocrit rises over weeks, and more red blood cells raise oxygen content; they are not a drive to breathe more.
Correct. Correcting the pH removes the central brake on ventilation.
Adults do not grow new alveoli in response to a week at altitude.
Breathing at altitude stays automatic, driven by the brainstem; it does not depend on conscious control.

why.correct: If arterial PCO2, PO2 and pH are nearly unchanged, the chemoreceptors are not seeing a large error signal. The rise comes mainly from signals from the motor cortex to the respiratory centers and from proprioceptors in moving limbs, with the chemoreceptors fine-tuning ventilation to hold PCO2 steady.
options: Arterial PO2 does not fall in moderate exercise, so the carotid bodies are not strongly stimulated by oxygen.
Carbon dioxide production rises several-fold. PCO2 stays steady because ventilation rises to match it.
Correct. The drive comes largely from central command and proprioceptors.
The Hering–Breuer reflex limits inspiration; it does not drive breathing up.

why.correct: Irritant receptors among the cells lining the airways respond to smoke, dust and fumes. Through the vagus nerves they trigger coughing, narrowing of the airways and rapid, shallow breathing.
options: Lung stretch receptors respond to inflation, not to smoke.
Central chemoreceptors respond to hydrogen ions in the brain's fluid, not to particles in the airways.
Correct. Irritant receptors cause coughing and bronchoconstriction.
The aortic bodies sense arterial blood chemistry, not smoke in the airways.

why.correct: In COPD, air leaves the lungs slowly, so FEV1 falls more than FVC. A ratio below 0.70, measured after a drug that opens the airways, shows obstruction that persists.
options: Correct. A low ratio that persists after the drug defines COPD's obstruction.
A high ratio means air leaves quickly for the volume moved, which fits normal lungs or restrictive disease, not obstruction.
A small total lung capacity is the mark of restrictive disease. In COPD, trapped air often makes it normal or larger.
A large improvement after albuterol points to reversible obstruction, as in asthma, and in any case vital capacity does not double.

why.correct: FEV1 ÷ FVC = 2.4 ÷ 4.0 = 0.60. That is below 0.70 after the airway-opening drug, so she has persistent airflow obstruction.
options: 1.67 comes from dividing FVC by FEV1, the wrong way round. FEV1 can never be larger than FVC, so the ratio is always below 1.
Correct. 0.60 is below the 0.70 cutoff.
The ratio is right, but 0.60 is below 0.70, so it is not normal.
0.85 does not follow from these numbers, and a ratio that high would not show obstruction.

why.correct: Destroying alveolar walls removes surface area and elastic fibers. Weaker recoil and loss of the outward pull on small airways make them collapse during expiration, so air is trapped, residual volume rises and FEV1 falls. The lungs become more compliant, not stiffer.

variables.name: Surface area for gas exchange
variables.why: Small alveoli merge into fewer, larger spaces, which have much less wall area, and the capillaries in the lost walls are gone.

variables.name: Elastic recoil of the lungs
variables.why: Protein-digesting enzymes have broken down the elastic fibers.

variables.name: Lung compliance
variables.why: With less elastic tissue to stretch, the lungs inflate more easily for a given pressure change.

variables.name: Residual volume
variables.why: Without elastic support, small airways collapse during expiration and trap air behind them.

variables.name: FEV1
variables.why: Collapsing airways and weak recoil slow the flow of air out during a forced breath.

why.correct: In emphysema, small airways collapse during expiration and trap air, so more air stays in the lungs after the fullest breath out. Residual volume, at the bottom of the scale, grows.
options: Tidal volume at rest is about normal or smaller. The trapped air is added below it, at the bottom of the scale.
Inspiratory reserve volume shrinks, because the lungs start each breath already overinflated.
Vital capacity falls, because trapped air takes up space that could otherwise be breathed in and out.
Correct. Trapped air enlarges the residual volume.

why.correct: The smallest airways have no cartilage. In healthy lungs, elastic fibers in the surrounding alveolar walls attach to their outside and pull them open. Emphysema destroys those fibers, so when pressure around the airways rises during expiration, they are squeezed shut.
options: Smooth muscle spasm is the mechanism of asthma, and it responds to drugs that open the airways. Emphysema's collapse does not.
Mucus plugging is the main problem in chronic bronchitis, not emphysema.
Correct. Loss of elastic support lets the airways collapse.
The smallest airways, the bronchioles, never had cartilage rings. They rely on the pull of surrounding tissue.

why.correct: Chronic bronchitis is defined by symptoms: a productive cough on most days for at least three months in each of two consecutive years, with no other cause.
options: Destruction of alveolar walls defines emphysema.
Wheezing that reverses fully is typical of asthma.
Infection of the alveoli with fever describes pneumonia.
Correct. The definition rests on a long-lasting cough with mucus.

why.correct: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, which lowers the surface for diffusion and removes elastic fibers, so compliance rises. A daily productive cough and enlarged mucus glands mark chronic bronchitis; fully reversible obstruction marks asthma.
options: Correct. This is the defining change of emphysema.
Correct. With less elastic tissue, the lungs stretch more easily.
A daily cough with mucus is the defining symptom of chronic bronchitis.
Correct. Losing alveolar walls and their capillaries shrinks the diffusion surface.
Emphysema's obstruction does not reverse with drugs that open the airways; asthma's largely does.
Enlarged mucus glands are a feature of chronic bronchitis.

why.correct: Asthma's obstruction comes largely from smooth muscle contraction, which albuterol relaxes through beta-2 receptor proteins, so the ratio returns toward normal. COPD's obstruction persists after the drug: collapsed airways and thickened, mucus-filled walls do not reverse.
options: This reverses the pattern. Emphysema's obstruction barely changes with albuterol; asthma's improves a lot.
Pulmonary edema does not usually produce a low ratio that corrects with albuterol; it mainly stiffens the lungs and floods alveoli.
Correct. Reversible obstruction fits asthma; persistent obstruction fits COPD.
Restrictive disease lowers volumes but keeps the ratio normal or high. Both ratios here are low.

why.correct: He is dangerously hypoxic and needs oxygen. Because large amounts can raise PCO2 in some people with severe COPD, mainly by worsening ventilation–perfusion mismatch and through the Haldane effect, oxygen is adjusted to a target saturation, often 88–92%, while his breathing and alertness are watched.
options: Oxygen is never withheld from a hypoxic patient. The hypoxic-drive explanation that many exams still teach plays at most a small part in the rise in PCO2.
Delaying oxygen leaves him severely hypoxic, which is far more dangerous than a controlled rise in PCO2.
Aiming for 100% can release hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction throughout his lungs and, with the Haldane effect, raise his PCO2. A lower target avoids this while correcting the hypoxemia.
Correct. Controlled oxygen to a target range treats the hypoxemia safely.

why.correct: Low alveolar oxygen throughout the lungs constricts pulmonary arterioles for years. Pulmonary artery pressure rises, the right ventricle pumps against a high afterload, thickens and eventually fails. This right-sided heart failure caused by lung disease is cor pulmonale; blood backs up into the systemic veins and fluid collects in the ankles.
options: Correct. Pulmonary hypertension from chronic hypoxia strains the right ventricle.
Left ventricular failure backs blood into the lungs, not the ankles, and it is not the usual link from COPD to the right heart.
Mucus stays in the airways; it does not enter the blood or the coronary arteries.
Polycythemia thickens the blood and adds to the workload, but it does not reduce filling of the right ventricle, and it is not the main cause.

why.correct: Long-term low blood oxygen makes the kidneys release more erythropoietin, which speeds erythropoiesis in the bone marrow. The red blood cell count and hematocrit rise: polycythemia.
options: Loss of water can concentrate the blood slightly, but a hematocrit this high in chronic hypoxemia comes from more red blood cells being made.
Carbon dioxide does not directly drive red blood cell production. The signal is low oxygen sensed by the kidneys.
Correct. This is the erythropoietin feedback loop responding to low oxygen.
Smoke does not act on the spleen to raise the red blood cell count.

why.correct: Her weak left ventricle cannot pump out all the blood reaching it. Pressure rises in the left atrium, the pulmonary veins and the pulmonary capillaries. Filtration then outpaces lymph drainage, and fluid collects first around the alveoli and then inside them: cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
options: A leaky membrane causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, as in sepsis or pneumonia. Her edema follows from heart failure.
Low colloid osmotic pressure adds to edema in some patients, but nothing here points to liver failure, and her heart failure explains it.
Lung lymphatics are working hard, not blocked. They are overwhelmed by the extra filtration.
Correct. High capillary pressure pushes fluid out: cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

why.correct: Carbon dioxide is about 20 times more soluble than oxygen, so it diffuses far more readily through a thickened, fluid-filled membrane. Oxygen transfer suffers first. The rapid breathing driven by sensory receptors in the alveolar walls also blows off carbon dioxide, keeping PCO2 normal or low.
options: Edema fluid is mostly water and plasma solutes; it does not react with oxygen.
Correct. Higher solubility lets carbon dioxide diffuse through the thicker barrier.
Carbon dioxide leaves the blood through the same respiratory membrane that oxygen crosses; there is no other route.
Fluid in the lung tissue does not change how hemoglobin releases carbon dioxide.

why.correct: Lying down moves blood from the legs and abdomen into the chest. More blood reaches the heart and lungs, but the failing left ventricle cannot pump it on, so pulmonary capillary pressure and edema increase. This is orthopnea, relieved by sitting up.
options: Correct. Extra venous return overloads the failing left side.
The chest wall and ribs hold their shape when you lie down; posture does not crush the lungs. The problem is the extra blood reaching the failing left side.
The diaphragm works when you lie down; you breathe normally in your sleep. Abdominal contents push on it a little, but that does not explain fluid building up in the lungs.
Posture does not change the protein concentration of the plasma.

why.correct: In noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, inflammation damages the capillary wall and the alveolar lining. Fluid and plasma proteins leak out even at normal pressure, and the protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli.
options: The question says his heart and capillary pressure are normal, which rules out the cardiogenic mechanism.
Correct. A leaky membrane lets fluid out at normal pressure.
Surfactant can be damaged in severe lung injury, but fever does not stop its production, and this is not the main cause of the fluid leak.
Air in the pleural cavity is a pneumothorax. It collapses the lung but does not fill the alveoli with fluid.

why.correct: The consolidated alveoli are full of inflammatory fluid, so blood flowing past them gets no air at all. Extra oxygen reaches only the healthy alveoli, and the blood there was already about 97% saturated, so it can carry little more. When the two streams mix, the unoxygenated blood still pulls the average down.
options: Correct. Blood that bypasses air cannot be helped by more oxygen in the air.
Bacteria use a trivial amount of oxygen compared with the oxygen passing through the lungs.
Oxygen does not block the respiratory centers.
Pneumonia does not change hemoglobin. Blood that reaches ventilated alveoli still loads oxygen normally.

why.correct: Tuberculosis is airborne. Alveolar macrophages take up the bacteria, which survive inside them. Weeks later, T cells activate the macrophages, and a granuloma contains the infection, often for life. If immunity later weakens, the dormant bacteria can reactivate.

Losing elastic fibers makes the lungs more compliant, not less: they stretch more easily and recoil less. Stiffer, less compliant lungs are a feature of restrictive disease such as pulmonary fibrosis.
options: This step is right. Smoke causes chronic inflammation in the lungs.
This step is right. The inflammatory cells release enzymes that digest proteins.
This step is right. Smoke tips the balance toward digestion by inactivating the protective protein.
This step is right. The enzymes destroy elastic fibers and alveolar walls.
This is the error. Emphysema raises lung compliance.
This step is right. Without elastic support, small airways collapse and trap air.

why.correct: Backed-up pressure reaches the pulmonary capillaries. Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes out more fluid than the lymphatics can remove.
options: Correct. Higher capillary pressure drives filtration into the lung tissue.
A higher colloid osmotic pressure would hold fluid in the blood, opposing edema.
Lymph flow rises, not stops, as the lymphatics try to keep up; edema forms when filtration exceeds even that raised flow.
A leaky membrane is the mechanism of noncardiogenic edema, not of edema from heart failure.

why.correct: A positive test shows her immune system has met the bacterium. With no symptoms and a normal X-ray, the bacteria are held in check in granulomas: latent infection. It does not spread to others, but treatment is often offered to prevent later activation.
options: Correct. Latent infection causes no symptoms and does not spread.
Active TB causes symptoms such as a long cough, fever and weight loss, and usually an abnormal X-ray.
A positive test in someone without symptoms usually means latent infection, not a false result.
A positive test does not mean pneumonia; she has no symptoms of lung infection.

why.correct: Narrowing the outlet at the lips keeps pressure inside the airways higher during expiration. That pressure pushes outward on the small airways, which have lost their elastic support, so they stay open longer and more trapped air escapes.
options: Pursed lips act during expiration, not on the air coming in.
Pursed-lip breathing does not strengthen the diaphragm; hyperinflation actually flattens and weakens it.
The air he breathes in is ordinary room air; pursing the lips on the way out does not change its oxygen.
Correct. Back-pressure splints the small airways open.

why.correct: A pulmonary embolism is a clot blocking a pulmonary artery. The alveoli beyond it are still ventilated but receive no blood, so they act as dead space.
options: In pneumonia, the alveoli fill with fluid but are still perfused: blood without air.
At the alveolar stage, fluid floods alveoli that are still perfused: blood without air.
Correct. Air reaches alveoli whose blood supply is blocked.
In asthma, narrowed airways reduce ventilation of alveoli that are still perfused: blood with too little air.
